key_terms.meaning: A controlled-switch circuit that converts a DC input into an AC output.
The stiff DC voltage rail, usually a capacitor, that feeds the inverter; its value sets the square-wave amplitude.
Two switches and a split DC bus form one leg; the load voltage swings between +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and −V<sub>dc</sub>/2.
Four switches in two legs; the load voltage swings between +V<sub>dc</sub> and −V<sub>dc</sub>.
Switches operate at the fundamental frequency and the output is a rectangular wave with odd harmonics.
Three legs switch one DC bus to produce three pole voltages spaced 120° apart.
Each switch conducts for 180°; three switches are on at any instant.
Each switch conducts for 120°; two switches are on at any instant and each phase has zero intervals.
One zero-voltage notch per half-cycle reduces the fundamental while the DC bus stays fixed.
Several equal notches per half-cycle control the fundamental and reduce low-order harmonics.
A sine reference compared with a triangular carrier makes the duty ratio vary sinusoidally.
Each leg switches between a DC rail and zero, so the load sees three voltage levels per cycle.
The load voltage alternates between +V<sub>dc</sub> and −V<sub>dc</sub> in every carrier cycle.
The reference voltage vector is built from two adjacent active states plus a zero state in each switching period.
A 60° region of the voltage-vector plane bounded by two adjacent active vectors.
Switching angles are chosen so selected low-order Fourier coefficients are exactly zero.
A large DC choke holds current constant and the bridge steers that current through the load.
Several voltage levels are stacked so the output steps are smaller and closer to a sine.
A control loop that estimates the grid voltage angle and frequency for synchronization.
A fast current loop forces the inverter current to follow a sine reference tied to the grid angle.

takeaways: A VSI switches the load between DC rails, so its unfiltered output is a rectangular wave whose amplitude and harmonic content are fixed by the bus and switching pattern.
Three-phase VSI operation is described by 60°-spaced states; 180° and 120° conduction differ in how many devices conduct and whether phase voltage has zero intervals.
Notch-based voltage control lowers the fundamental by removing voltage-time area while keeping the DC bus unchanged.
SPWM moves harmonics to the carrier frequency and makes the fundamental proportional to the reference amplitude.
SVM uses the same bridge states as SPWM but chooses dwell times geometrically, giving better DC-bus utilization and lower harmonic current.
Harmonic elimination places switching angles to null chosen low-order harmonics, at the cost of solving nonlinear angle equations offline.
A CSI needs a stiff DC current and uses load or forced commutation; it is suited to high-power rugged loads but cannot freewheel through antiparallel diodes.
Multilevel inverters reduce voltage steps, device voltage stress, and harmonic content by adding levels.
A grid-tied inverter controls current, not voltage: the PLL supplies the grid angle and the current loop tracks a sine reference.
bank_note: Long answers usually expect circuit diagrams, switching tables, waveform reasoning, and a clear comparison of modulation methods and inverter types.

Check minimum pulse width and harmonic spectrum

bank.q: For a three-phase VSI, use space vector modulation to place a reference vector in sector I. Explain how the two active-state times and zero-state time are found and used to generate switching signals.

bank.q: Compare bipolar and unipolar sinusoidal PWM for a single-phase full-bridge inverter in terms of output levels, harmonic spectrum, switching losses, and filter requirement.

bank.q: A grid-tied inverter must inject a sinusoidal current into a weak grid. Discuss how a PLL, current controller, and DC-link voltage loop work together, and what happens if the grid angle estimate is wrong.
outline: Current reference from power and angle

bank.q: Evaluate multilevel inverters against a two-level VSI for a medium-voltage motor drive. Cover device voltage stress, harmonic content, component count, and control complexity.
Choose between a VSI and a CSI for an application that needs rugged short-circuit behavior and high power. Justify the choice using commutation, DC-link energy storage, and load compatibility.
outline: VSI uses capacitor DC link and antiparallel diodes
CSI uses choke and limits current rise
CSI needs commutation and suits motor loads
VSI is common for general AC loads

glossary.def: A power electronic converter that changes DC into AC by controlled switching.
An inverter whose DC link is held at a stiff voltage, usually by a capacitor, so the output voltage is set by switching.
An inverter whose DC link is held at a stiff current, usually by an inductor, so the output current is set by switching.
A single-leg inverter with two switches and a split DC bus that produces two output levels.
A two-leg inverter with four switches that applies positive, negative, or zero voltage to the load.
The voltage at a leg midpoint measured with respect to the DC-bus midpoint.
The difference between two pole voltages in a three-phase inverter.
The electrical angle interval during which a switch is kept on.
In sine-triangle PWM, the ratio of sine reference peak to triangular carrier peak; it sets the fundamental output in the linear range.
The frequency of the triangular wave in PWM, which sets the switching frequency.
The fraction of a switching period for which a switch is on.
A PWM method where each leg switches between a DC rail and zero, giving three load voltage levels.
A PWM method where the load voltage switches between +V<sub>dc</sub> and −V<sub>dc</sub>.
A complex-number representation of the three phase voltages obtained by the Clarke transform.
One of six 60° regions in the space vector plane, bounded by two adjacent active vectors.
The time spent in a chosen switching state during one sampling period.
A switching-angle design method that makes selected Fourier coefficients zero.
The RMS value of all non-fundamental harmonics divided by the RMS fundamental, often given as a percentage.
An inverter that produces more than two voltage levels so the output approaches a sine in small steps.
A multilevel inverter that uses clamping diodes and a split DC bus to create a zero level and share voltage stress.
A control loop that estimates the phase and frequency of the grid voltage.
An inverter that injects power into an AC grid and stays synchronized with the grid voltage.
Protection that stops a grid-tied inverter from energizing a disconnected grid section.
An inductor in the DC link of a current source inverter that keeps the DC current nearly constant.
An antiparallel diode that carries inductive load current when its switch turns off.
